sections.h2: What you can put in a QR code
paras: A QR code stores text. A camera app reads it and decides what to do: a web address opens in the browser, a phone number offers to call, an email address offers to write a message, and anything else is shown as text. So this generator works for a message, a contact detail, a product code, a short note, an address or a coupon code.
For a web address, use URL to QR code, which tidies the link for you. For a Wi-Fi network that guests can join with one scan, use the Wi-Fi QR code generator.

sections.h2: Make a code that scans every time
paras: Keep the text short. More text means a denser code with smaller squares, which is harder to scan from far away or on a poor print. Use a dark code on a light background. Light-on-dark codes fail on many scanners. Leave the quiet zone. The blank border around the code is part of the code, and four squares wide is the standard.

The error correction level lets a code survive damage or a logo placed on top, but higher levels make the code denser. Medium (15 percent) suits most uses; choose High only if the code will be scuffed or partly covered. Always test the finished code with a phone before you print a thousand copies.

sections.h2: PNG or SVG, and what size?
paras: A PNG is a normal picture: good for slides, websites and documents. Choose a size that is at least as big as the space it will fill, because enlarging a small PNG makes the edges blurry. An SVG is drawn with shapes, so it stays sharp at any size: use it for posters, packaging and signs, and send it to your printer.

For print, make the code at least about 2 cm (0.8 inch) wide, and bigger if people will scan it from a distance. A rough rule is that the scanning distance should be no more than ten times the width of the code.

sections.h2: Static codes: no expiry, no tracking
paras: The code you make here contains your text itself, so it never expires, needs no account and works as long as the thing it points to exists. Nothing is stored on our servers, and we cannot see how many people scan it. If you need scan statistics, you would need a service that redirects through its own address, which adds a dependency that can expire or be switched off.

faq.q: Is this QR code generator really free?
faq.a: Yes. There is no sign-up, no watermark and no limit. The code is generated in your browser, so it costs nothing to run and nothing is stored.
No. The code contains your text itself, so it works forever. Only a code that points to a third-party redirect address can stop working.

faq.q: How much text fits in a QR code?
faq.a: A lot less than a page: roughly 2,900 characters at the lowest error correction, and fewer at higher levels or with non-Latin characters. Shorter text gives a simpler code that scans more easily.

faq.q: Can I use it for Japanese, Chinese or emoji?
faq.a: Yes. The text is encoded as UTF-8, so any language and emoji work, although they use more space than plain English letters.

faq.q: Should I download PNG or SVG?
faq.a: Use PNG for screens and documents and SVG for print, because an SVG stays sharp at any size.
No. The QR code is built in your browser, and nothing you type is sent to a server.

sections.h2: A QR code for any link
paras: A QR code for a link is the quickest way to move a web address from a screen or a page onto a phone. People point the camera at it and tap the banner that appears: no typing, no typos. It works for a website, a menu, a social profile, a form, a map location, a video, an app store page or a download.

This tool checks the address as you type. It adds https:// when you leave it out, refuses links that could run code (such as javascript:), and warns if the address has spaces or does not look like a web address. You can also make codes for mailto: and tel: links.

The longer the address, the more squares the code needs, and the harder it is to scan from a distance. If your link has long tracking parameters, shorten it first or link to a simpler page. A short address also helps if someone has to type it because a camera fails. Before you print, check that the page loads quickly on a phone, because that is where most scans happen.

The code made here holds the address itself. It never expires and works without any account, but it also cannot count scans, because it does not pass through a server. If you need to measure scans, add tracking parameters such as utm_source to the address, and read the results in your own analytics. Be careful with services that put their own redirect address in the code: if the service stops or the plan ends, every printed code breaks.

sections.h2: Where to use a link QR code
paras: Restaurant menus, posters, flyers, business cards, product packaging, event tickets, shop windows, slides, name badges and lecture handouts. Place the code where people can reach it, give it a clear call to action such as "Scan for the menu", and keep the quiet zone around it free of text and patterns.

faq.q: How do I make a QR code for a link?
faq.a: Paste the address into the box. The QR code appears straight away. Test it with your phone, then download the PNG or SVG.

faq.q: Does a QR code for a URL expire?
faq.a: Not one made here. The code contains the address itself, so it keeps working for as long as the page exists.

faq.q: Can I see how many people scanned it?
faq.a: Not from the code itself, because it does not pass through any server. Add tracking parameters to the address and read them in your analytics.

faq.q: Do I need to type https://?
faq.a: No. If you leave it out, https:// is added automatically. Type http:// yourself only if the site really does not support https.

faq.q: Is it safe to scan unknown QR codes?
faq.a: Take care: a code can point to any address. Look at the address your phone shows before you open it, and do not enter passwords on pages you reached by an unfamiliar code.

faq.q: Is the link sent to your servers?
faq.a: No. The code is generated in your browser, and the address is not uploaded or stored.

wifi.title: Wi-Fi QR Code Generator: Share Your Wi-Fi Password With a Scan
wifi.description: Make a Wi-Fi QR code so guests join your network by scanning, with no typing. Works on iPhone and Android. Free, and the password never leaves your browser.
wifi.lead: Create a QR code that connects a phone to your Wi-Fi in one scan. Enter the network name and password, download the code and print it. The password stays in your browser.
steps: Enter the network name (SSID) exactly as it appears on your phone, including capital letters.
Enter the password and choose the security type. Most networks are WPA / WPA2 / WPA3. Tick the box if the network is hidden.
Scan the preview with a phone camera. The phone should offer to join the network. Press Download PNG or Download SVG.
Print it or show it on a screen where guests can scan it.

sections.h2: How a Wi-Fi QR code works
paras: The code contains a short line of text that describes your network: its name, its password, its security type, and whether it is hidden. It looks like WIFI:T:WPA;S:MyNetwork;P:mypassword;;. The camera app on a recent iPhone or Android phone recognises that format and offers to join the network, so the guest never has to read out or type a long password. Special characters such as semicolons, commas, colons, quotation marks and backslashes are escaped for you, so unusual passwords work.
Very old phones and some third-party camera apps may not understand the format. In that case, a guest can still scan the code with a QR reader app, or you can show the password as text as well.

Your password is used only in your browser to draw the code. It is not uploaded, stored or logged. But anyone who scans the printed code gets the password, so decide where the code goes. Do not put your main network's code in a public place. A guest network is a better choice for a code on a wall: it separates visitors from your own devices, you can change its password without disconnecting your own things, and many routers can switch it off with one setting.
If the code was shared more widely than you meant, change the password on the router and make a new code. The guide to sharing a Wi-Fi password safely covers guest networks and other options.

Choose WPA / WPA2 / WPA3 for almost every network made in the last ten years. Choose WEP only for a very old router, and consider replacing it, because WEP is weak. Choose No password for an open network, such as a public hotspot. If your network does not broadcast its name, tick hidden network so the phone knows to look for it.

sections.h2: If the code does not connect
paras: Check the network name and password for typos, including capital letters and look-alike characters such as 0 and O. Make sure the security type matches your router. Check that the code is large and well lit, with the quiet zone around it. Some corporate and school networks use personal logins that a QR code cannot hold, and those cannot be joined this way.

faq.q: How do I make a QR code for my Wi-Fi?
faq.a: Enter the network name and password, choose the security type and press Download. Guests then scan the code with the camera app and tap to join.

faq.q: Does it work on both iPhone and Android?
faq.a: Yes, on recent versions the built-in camera app reads the Wi-Fi format and offers to join. Very old phones may need a QR reader app.

faq.q: Is my Wi-Fi password sent to your servers?
faq.a: No. The password is used in your browser to draw the code and is never uploaded or stored. Anyone who scans the code, however, gets the password, so place it carefully.

faq.q: Should I put my main network on a poster?
faq.a: It is better to use a guest network for any code that many people can see. You can change the guest password without disconnecting your own devices.

faq.q: What if my password has special characters?
faq.a: The generator escapes semicolons, commas, colons, quotation marks and backslashes for you, so unusual passwords still work.

faq.q: Can I make a code for a hidden network?
faq.a: Yes. Tick the hidden network box so the phone knows to look for it even though the network does not broadcast its name.
